New machine. Its objects are: riliper, migapus, famagin, vubidan, belonek, ninives.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: riliper, migapus, famagin
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group of three did not light the machine, but I don't yet know the rule. If any single nexiom lights it, both nexioms must be among the other three. I'll test those three directly to check that.

TEST: vubidan, belonek, ninives
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither half lit the machine. So a single nexiom alone is not enough. The likeliest rule is that the machine lights only when both nexioms are on it together. That would mean one nexiom is in {riliper, migapus, famagin} and the other is in {vubidan, belonek, ninives}, which leaves 9 possible pairs. I'll test two from each group. A light would cut the pairs to 4, and no light would leave 5.

TEST: riliper, migapus, vubidan, belonek
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

The machine lit up with riliper, migapus, vubidan and belonek, but not with either group of three. The likeliest rule is that it lights only when both nexioms are on it. If so, one nexiom is riliper or migapus, and the other is vubidan or belonek, which leaves 4 possible pairs.

This test includes riliper and migapus, so one nexiom is guaranteed to be on the machine. It should therefore light up only if vubidan is the second nexiom; otherwise the second one is belonek. My last test will then decide between riliper and migapus.

There is a less likely rule I can't fully rule out: the machine lights when exactly one nexiom is present. Two tests can't separate every pair under both rules, so I'm going with the more likely one.

TEST: riliper, migapus, vubidan
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

No light with riliper, migapus and vubidan. Under the "both nexioms needed" rule, one of riliper or migapus is a nexiom, so vubidan must not be the second one. That makes belonek the second nexiom.

The first nexiom is either riliper or migapus. I'll put riliper on with belonek. If it lights, the pair is riliper and belonek. If not, it's migapus and belonek.

TEST: riliper, belonek
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Under the "lights only when both nexioms are on it" rule, all five results fit migapus and belonek:

- **Test 1** (riliper, migapus, famagin) has only migapus, so no light.
- **Test 2** (vubidan, belonek, ninives) has only belonek, so no light.
- **Test 3** (riliper, migapus, vubidan, belonek) has both, so it lit.
- **Test 4** (riliper, migapus, vubidan) has only migapus, so no light.
- **Test 5** (riliper, belonek) has only belonek, so no light.

I also checked the other rule I mentioned, that the machine lights when exactly one nexiom is present. Tests 1 to 4 leave belonek and ninives as the only pair that rule could allow. But that pair would have made test 5 light, and it didn't. So the results rule that out, and the answer doesn't depend on my earlier guess about the rule.

ANSWER: nexioms = migapus, belonek
One last question. If only belonek were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

No, it would not light up.

If my answer is right, vubidan and ninives are not nexioms. Since non-nexioms never affect the machine, test 2 (vubidan, belonek, ninives) was the same as putting belonek on by itself, and it did not light. Test 5 (riliper, belonek) shows the same thing, because riliper is also not a nexiom.

This follows directly from the results and does not depend on which rule the machine uses. It does depend on migapus and belonek being the correct pair.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: lidenol, vufanir, kusazu, natuma, girufik, gilavos.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects.

TEST: lidenol, vufanir, kusazu
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group lit up. Next I'll test the other three objects, to see whether that group can trigger the machine as well.

TEST: natuma, girufik, gilavos
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group of three lit up and the other three did not. So under the simplest rules (the machine lights when either nexiom is present, or only when both are), both nexioms are among lidenol, vufanir and kusazu. Rules like "lights with exactly one nexiom" are ruled out, because then both groups would have lit.

Next I'll test the pair lidenol and vufanir.
- If it does not light, the machine must need both nexioms, and they are lidenol + kusazu or vufanir + kusazu. One more test will settle which.
- If it does light, I'll use single-object tests to tell the two rules apart and find the pair.

TEST: lidenol, vufanir
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

The pair lidenol and vufanir did not light. That rules out the "either nexiom is enough" rule. Under that rule, both nexioms would have to be among the first three objects (since the second group stayed dark). But neither lidenol nor vufanir triggered the machine, which leaves only kusazu, and two nexioms are required.

So the machine most likely needs both nexioms present. Kusazu must be one of them. The other is either lidenol or vufanir.

If kusazu and lidenol light up together, those are the nexioms. If not, the pair is kusazu and vufanir.

TEST: kusazu, lidenol
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

The results so far fit the rule "lights only when both nexioms are present", with the nexioms being kusazu and lidenol.

One less likely rule also fits. Kusazu could light the machine by itself, while a "blocker" nexiom among natuma, girufik and gilavos stops it from lighting. That would explain why the second group stayed dark.

Testing kusazu alone tells these apart. If it stays dark, the answer is kusazu and lidenol. If it lights, the blocker rule holds instead, and I would have to guess which of the three is the blocker.

TEST: kusazu
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

All five results fit the rule "the machine lights only when both nexioms are present," with kusazu and lidenol as the nexioms:

- **Test 1:** lidenol, vufanir and kusazu lit up, because both nexioms were there.
- **Test 2:** natuma, girufik and gilavos stayed dark, because neither nexiom was there.
- **Test 3:** lidenol and vufanir stayed dark, because kusazu was missing.
- **Test 4:** kusazu and lidenol lit up, because both nexioms were there.
- **Test 5:** kusazu alone stayed dark, because lidenol was missing. This rules out the "blocker" idea, where kusazu lights the machine by itself.

One more complicated explanation is still possible, though I think it is unlikely. Lidenol could light the machine by itself, with vufanir acting as a blocker. That would also explain tests 1 and 3, and the leftover rule ("lights with both nexioms") explains the rest more simply.

ANSWER: nexioms = kusazu, lidenol
One last question. If only kusazu were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

No. This one I don't need to infer, because I observed it directly: test 5 put kusazu alone on the machine, and it did not light up. That also fits the rule I settled on, where the machine lights only when both nexioms (kusazu and lidenol) are present together.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: ludekor, tumeduk, gemoton, bibavu, kinidos, kirevin.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: ludekor, tumeduk, gemoton
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first three lit up. Next I'll test the other three, which helps show whether the machine needs one nexiom or both to light.

TEST: bibavu, kinidos, kirevin
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group (ludekor, tumeduk, gemoton) lit up and the second group did not. If the machine lights when any nexiom is present, or only when both are present, then both nexioms are in the first group. That leaves three possible pairs: ludekor+tumeduk, ludekor+gemoton or tumeduk+gemoton. Testing ludekor alone helps separate these. If it lights, the rule is "any nexiom" and ludekor is one of the pair. If it doesn't, either the pair is tumeduk+gemoton or the machine needs both nexioms.

TEST: ludekor
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Since the first group lit and the second did not, both nexioms should be among ludekor, tumeduk and gemoton. (If the rule were "exactly one nexiom lights it", one nexiom would sit in each group and both tests would have lit.)

Four cases remain:
- **Any nexiom lights it:** ludekor alone did not light, so the pair would be tumeduk + gemoton.
- **Both nexioms are needed:** the pair could be ludekor + tumeduk, ludekor + gemoton or tumeduk + gemoton.

Testing ludekor + tumeduk splits these evenly:
- **If it lights:** the case is either "any nexiom" with tumeduk + gemoton, or "both needed" with ludekor + tumeduk. Testing tumeduk alone would then tell them apart.
- **If it doesn't light:** the case is either "both needed" with ludekor + gemoton or with tumeduk + gemoton. Testing ludekor + gemoton would then tell them apart.

TEST: ludekor, tumeduk
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

The pair ludekor + tumeduk did not light. That rules out "any nexiom lights it" with tumeduk + gemoton, because tumeduk alone would have lit it. It also rules out "both needed" with ludekor + tumeduk.

So the machine needs both nexioms, and the pair is either ludekor + gemoton or tumeduk + gemoton.

- **If ludekor + gemoton lights:** the nexioms are ludekor and gemoton.
- **If it doesn't light:** the nexioms are tumeduk and gemoton.

TEST: ludekor, gemoton
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

The tests point to a machine that lights only when **both** nexioms are on it, and the pair is tumeduk and gemoton.

1. The first three objects (ludekor, tumeduk, gemoton) lit up and the other three did not. So both nexioms are among the first three.
2. Ludekor + tumeduk did not light. If one nexiom were enough, tumeduk would have lit it, since tumeduk must be a nexiom in that case. So the machine needs both nexioms.
3. The pair cannot be ludekor + tumeduk, because that pair did not light.
4. Ludekor + gemoton also did not light, so that pair is ruled out.
5. Tumeduk + gemoton is the only pair left. It fits every result, including the first group lighting up.

I assumed the machine responds to how many nexioms are on it. I also checked rules where only one particular nexiom matters, and none of them fit all five results.

ANSWER: nexioms = tumeduk, gemoton
One last question. If only gemoton were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**No.**

Ludekor + gemoton did not light up. Under my answer, ludekor is not a nexiom, and objects that are not nexioms never affect the machine. So putting gemoton on alone should give the same result as ludekor + gemoton: no light.

This also matches the rule the tests point to, that the machine lights only when both nexioms are present. Gemoton alone is only one of them.

The prediction depends on the answer being right. If ludekor were actually a nexiom, the argument from ludekor + gemoton would not hold.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: vitado, maluzu, mapenu, kezokil, dekemar, fibemu.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects together to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: vitado, maluzu, mapenu
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group lit up, so at least one nexiom is likely among vitado, maluzu and mapenu. I don't yet know the machine's rule; for example, it might need one nexiom, both, or exactly one. Testing the other three objects should help tell those cases apart.

TEST: kezokil, dekemar, fibemu
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The second group did not light up, which rules out a rule where exactly one nexiom triggers the machine. If one nexiom were in each group, the second group would have lit too. So most likely both nexioms are among vitado, maluzu and mapenu. The machine probably lights up when any nexiom is present ("any" rule) or only when both are present ("both" rule).

Testing vitado and maluzu together helps separate these:
- **If it does not light:** the rule must be "both", and the pair is either vitado+mapenu or maluzu+mapenu. One more test will settle it.
- **If it lights:** either the rule is "any" (and the pair could be any two of the three), or the rule is "both" and the pair is vitado+maluzu. Testing single objects next will sort that out.

TEST: vitado, maluzu
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

The third test lit up, so the possibilities are:
- **"Any" rule:** the machine lights whenever at least one nexiom is present. Since kezokil, dekemar and fibemu did not light it, both nexioms are among the first three. The pair could be vitado+maluzu, vitado+mapenu or maluzu+mapenu.
- **"Both" rule:** the machine lights only when both nexioms are present. Then the pair must be vitado+maluzu.

That leaves four likely cases. Testing vitado alone splits them in half:
- **If it lights:** the rule is "any" and the pair is vitado+maluzu or vitado+mapenu. Testing maluzu alone would then settle it.
- **If it does not light:** the case is either "any" with maluzu+mapenu, or "both" with vitado+maluzu. Testing maluzu alone would separate those two as well.

I'm setting aside stranger rules, such as the machine lighting only when no nexiom is present. Those would put both nexioms in the second group, but two tests cannot cover every case.

TEST: vitado
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Vitado alone did not light up. Under the "any" rule (lights with at least one nexiom), that means vitado is not a nexiom, so the pair is maluzu+mapenu. Under the "both" rule (lights only with both nexioms), the pair is vitado+maluzu, and one nexiom alone would not light the machine.

Testing mapenu alone separates these two cases:
- **If it lights:** the rule is "any" and the nexioms are maluzu and mapenu.
- **If it does not light:** the rule is "both" and the nexioms are vitado and maluzu.

TEST: mapenu
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Mapenu alone did not light up, which rules out the "any" rule. Under that rule the pair would be maluzu and mapenu, and mapenu alone would have lit the machine.

That leaves the "both" rule: the machine lights only when both nexioms are present. Under that rule the pair is vitado and maluzu, and it fits every result:
- **vitado, maluzu, mapenu:** both nexioms present, so it lit.
- **kezokil, dekemar, fibemu:** no nexioms present, so it did not light.
- **vitado, maluzu:** both present, so it lit.
- **vitado alone:** only one nexiom, so it did not light.
- **mapenu alone:** no nexiom, so it did not light.

The "exactly one" rule is also ruled out. Under it, maluzu would have to be the only nexiom in the first group, so the other nexiom would be in the second group, and that group would have lit up.

ANSWER: nexioms = vitado, maluzu
One last question. If only maluzu were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

No, maluzu alone would not light the machine. The results only fit a machine that lights when both nexioms are present, with vitado and maluzu as the pair. Maluzu by itself is just one nexiom, so under that rule it would stay dark.

I never actually tested maluzu alone, so this is an inference rather than an observation. Still, the other simple rules all clash with at least one result:
- **"Any nexiom lights it":** vitado alone would then have to be a non-nexiom. That makes the pair maluzu and mapenu, but mapenu alone did not light.
- **"Exactly one nexiom lights it":** the second group would have had to light up, and it did not.

PROBE: no
